retail_intro: On the eve of a possible invasion the dominant narrative is buy-the-dip faith, the conviction that geopolitical selloffs are sold on the threat and bought on the resolution, now applied with leverage as analysts start publishing buy lists after the correction [[n1719]].

retail.title: 3x Nasdaq 100 ETF / TQQQ — buying the invasion scare, three times over
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The story the crowd is telling itself is the simplest one in markets: geopolitical selloffs are gifts, and the bigger the fear, the better the entry. With the S&P 500 in its first correction in two years [[n1908]], the dip-buying reflex has a fresh target, and for the most aggressive accounts the obvious vehicle is the triple-leveraged Nasdaq 100 fund. TQQQ closed at $45.14, down 7.65% in a single session and 21.22% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). That is the kind of number that turns fear into FOMO: if the Nasdaq merely retraces its week, a leveraged wrapper promises the fastest rebound on the board. The hook is faith: every scare gets bought, and whoever blinks sells the low.
What Is Driving It

The trigger is Ukraine. The ruble plummeted 3% and Russian bonds were hammered as Ukraine declared a state of emergency [[n1281]], while satellite photos show Russian forces and supplies being bolstered around the country amid fears of a full-scale invasion [[n1282]]. US equities absorbed it badly: the S&P 500 fell 1.84% to 4,225.50 index points and is down 5.49% over five sessions, the Nasdaq 100 lost 2.60% to 13,509.43 index points and 7.60% over five, and the VIX jumped 2.21 points to 31.02 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). Rates offer no relief: the 2Y yield sits at 1.58%, up 56 bps over 20 observations in a bear flattening (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-23), and the Fed is expected to raise rates in March, with calls for 50 bps growing louder [[n1801]]. That combination makes the dip feel big enough to buy.
The Social Signal

The coverage has moved from whether to buy to what to buy. Business Insider is running Mark Mahaney's top three tech stocks to buy after the correction [[n1719]], UKTN is publishing the best stocks and shares to buy today [[n1593]], and Canstar is explaining what buying the dip is and whether it is worth it [[n1533]]. That is attention that precedes dip-buying, not capitulation: shopping lists, not exit plans. The counter-signal sits in the broker that defined the era: Robinhood closed at $10.86, down 20.56% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23), a hint that the market doubts how long the retail bid lasts.
Historical Analog

The template is explicit. After the S&P 500's first correction in two years, MarketWatch went straight to what history says happens next [[n1908]], and the New York Times framed the slide as stocks hitting correction territory as governments announced sanctions against Russia [[n0640]]. Retail is betting on the familiar mechanism: shocks that do not dent earnings tend to be sold on the threat and bought once uncertainty resolves. The flaw in applying it to TQQQ is mechanical, not historical. The fund resets its leverage daily, so its path depends on the sequence of moves, not just the destination: over five sessions it fell 21.22% while the Nasdaq 100 fell 7.60% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). In a choppy, two-way tape that reset erodes value, so an index recovery does not guarantee a fund recovery.
Smart Money View

The professional split is wide. On the bullish side, Raymond James says buy the dip in Fastly, which it sees rebounding more than 80% [[n0445]], and MarketWatch flagged the correction's first bullish divergence chart signal [[n1909]]. Against them, Wall Street banks fear inflation, asset-price deflation and even recession [[n0093]], and MarketWatch's own warning is that whether Fed hikes crush the market depends on their speed [[n1850]]. For a leveraged holder the bears have the stronger point: the Fed is tightening into the drawdown, not rescuing it.
When the Narrative Breaks

The trade dies if the threat becomes an event. Russia says the Donbass separatists have asked Putin for military help [[n1278]], and a full-scale attack would turn a valuation dip into a repricing of energy, sanctions and growth at once. The observable line is the S&P 500's 4,225.50 close: a further break with the VIX pushing above 31.02 would tell dip-buyers the low is not in (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). Leverage is the accelerant, and The Reformed Broker argues options expiration keeps crushing the stock market [[n1571]], a reminder that positioning, not just news, can force the next leg. One clean invalidation: an invasion that lifts volatility instead of resolving uncertainty, so the daily reset works against the buyer.

retail.title: Aerospace & Defense ETF / ITA — buying the arsenal and the target
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The war trade has two legs, and ETF investors are buying both: the Financial Times reports ETF investors piling into Russian equities and defence stocks [[n0837]]. The Russia leg is the contrarian's lottery ticket. Russian markets plunged on the recognition of the separatist regions and then pared losses [[n1245]], and Market Realist is fielding the curious with an explainer on who owns Lukoil [[n0782]]. The defence leg is the hedge: Lockheed Martin rose 0.70% to $388.90 and is up 1.75% over five sessions, and General Dynamics gained 1.64% over the same five sessions in which the S&P 500 lost 5.49% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23).
Where It Breaks

The two legs cannot both win in the scenario that matters. If sanctions escalate from targeted to systemic, the damage lands on the Russian leg, where the ruble and bonds are already under fire [[n1281]] and Warren Buffett avoids Russia over threats of violence and asset seizure [[n0658]]. The defence leg is no sure thing either: the broader ITA fund fell 1.14% to $101.69 and 3.98% over five sessions, and Raytheon Technologies and Northrop Grumman both fell on the day (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). Watch whether Lockheed holds $388.90 if equities break lower.

retail.title: Palantir Technologies / PLTR — the war-tech favourite still falling
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Palantir's fans have always sold it as the software of national security, and its chief executive just handed them a line for a war scare: bad times are good for Palantir, Alex Karp says, in a Diginomica piece that also notes a tumbling share price [[n0558]]. The government pipeline keeps filling, with Reuters reporting the CDC tapped Palantir to support the US COVID-19 drug supply [[n0564]]. Yet the stock closed at $10.43, down 0.48% on the day, 26.39% over five sessions and 20.14% over twenty (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). For believers, a defence-adjacent name at a crash price is the war trade with upside.
Where It Breaks

The market is still pricing the cost side of the story, because Karp's optimism arrives alongside increased losses [[n0558]]. With the 2Y yield up 56 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-23), a loss-making growth stock is fighting the rate tape. Government work is lumpy and slow; a war scare does not become contracts within a news cycle. The level to reclaim is the $13.06 close of twenty sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23); until then, Karp's line is a slogan, not a floor.

retail.title: Wheat / ZW=F — the breadbasket war premium
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The war trade's most visceral leg sits on the dinner table. CNBC is explaining how an invasion of Ukraine, the breadbasket of Europe, could hit supply chains [[n1703]], and Reuters reports deepening tensions seen curbing food supplies and lifting prices [[n0571]]. CBOT wheat closed at 876.00 US cents a bushel, up 3.76% on the day and 12.34% over five sessions, with corn up 7.17% and soybeans 7.98% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). Successful Farming's Wednesday tape, soybeans 40¢ higher and wheat up 32¢ [[n1714]], is the kind of print that makes food inflation feel tradable.
Where It Breaks

This is a premium on a scenario, not yet a shortage, so de-escalation is the obvious killer. The second-order trade is moving too: Bloomberg warns fertilizer shortages tied to the tension may hit the US growing season [[n0715]], and Mosaic rose 2.29% on the day (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23). Retail exposure typically comes through futures-based funds that roll contracts and can trail the front month. Watch 818.00 US cents, the close of twenty sessions earlier: a slide toward it means the premium is gone (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-23).
